Lecture 11 - Radiation and acoustic environment: Problems 11, worked

34870 Electroacoustics | 2 November 2026 | Finn Agerkvist
How to read this: every step first states the formula, then the MATLAB line is that same formula typed in, and the result appears right below it.
Official solutions (34870Solutions11.pdf, 3-Nov) cover Problems 1 and 2 only, and they agree with this script: the same network, a flat 84-85 dB of power below the knee, and an efficiency of about 0.3 %. One difference: the official polar plots use 1.5, 3 and 6 kHz, while the sheet asks for 5 kHz; this script follows the sheet. There is no official solution for Problem 3 (diffrac).
The sheet's header says "Problems 10"; it is the sheet filed with lecture 11 (34870-Problems11.pdf, dated 30-Oct). diffrac.m (Problem 3) is in this folder.
Air (from the sheet):
rho = 1.2 % air density [kg/m^3]
rho = 1.2000
c = 344 % speed of sound [m/s]
c = 344
 
% Figures for the vault note are written here when the folder exists:
imgDir = fullfile(getenv('HOME'), 'DTU', 'Obsidian', 'Courses', ...
'34870 Electroacoustics', 'Images', 'Lecture11');

The formulas used in this problem set (slides 15-22)

Piston in an infinite baffle, far field. Adding up the point sources on the piston gives the on-axis monopole-like term times a directivity:
Directivity function (depends on frequency and radius only through ka):
Radiated power from the volume velocity U and the real part of the radiation impedance:
Symbols: a piston radius [m], k = omega/c wavenumber [1/m], U volume velocity [m^3/s] (Jacobsen calls it Q; the slides use U, as here), J_1 the Bessel function of the first kind, order 1 (MATLAB: besselj(1, x)).

Problem 1 - Directivity of a 6 cm piston at 1.5, 3 and 5 kHz

a1 = 0.06 % piston radius [m]
a1 = 0.0600
f1 = [1500 3000 5000] % frequencies [Hz]
f1 = 1×3
1500 3000 5000
Size against wavelength. The piston starts to beam once ka is about 1, and the first null appears when ka sin(theta) reaches the first zero of J_1, which is 3.832:
ka1 = 2*pi*f1*a1/c
ka1 = 1×3
1.6439 3.2877 5.4795
So 1.5 kHz is mildly directive (ka = 1.64, no null), 3 kHz is close to the edge (ka = 3.29 < 3.83, still no null in front), and 5 kHz has a null and a side lobe (ka = 5.48).
Angle of the first null (only where ka > 3.832):
theta0_5k = asind(3.832/ka1(3)) % [deg]
theta0_5k = 44.3734
-6 dB half-angle. D = 0.5 when the argument x = ka sin(theta) solves 2J_1(x)/x = 0.5, i.e. x = 2.215:
x6 = fzero(@(x) 2*besselj(1,x)./x - 0.5, 2)
x6 = 2.2151
theta6 = asind(min(x6./ka1, 1)) % [deg], 90 means "never down 6 dB"
theta6 = 1×3
90.0000 42.3570 23.8441
Directivity on a grid of angles. sin(theta) = 0 at the front gives 0/0; the limit is 1, so a tiny offset avoids the NaN:
theta = linspace(-pi/2, pi/2, 721); % front half-plane (baffle)
x = ka1(:) * sin(theta) + eps; % rows = frequencies
D = 2*besselj(1, x)./x;
DdB = 20*log10(abs(D));
Polar plot. As the sheet hints, a negative dB value as a radius flips the plot. Choose a dynamic range (40 dB) and plot DdB + 40, clipped at 0:
range = 40;
R = max(DdB + range, 0);
fig1 = figure('Name', 'L11_P1_directivity');
theme(fig1, 'light');
polarplot(theta, R, 'LineWidth', 1.5); % one line per row of R
ax = gca;
ax.ThetaZeroLocation = 'top'; ax.ThetaLim = [-90 90];
ax.RLim = [0 range]; ax.RTick = 0:10:range;
ax.RTickLabel = string((0:10:range) - range) + " dB";
legend(compose('%.1f kHz (ka = %.2f)', f1'/1e3, ka1'), 'Location', 'southoutside');
title('Problem 1: piston in a baffle, a = 6 cm');
if saveFigs, exportgraphics(fig1, fullfile(imgDir, 'L11_P1_directivity.png'), 'Resolution', 150); end
Reading the plot: at 1.5 kHz the response is down only about 3 dB at 90 degrees, at 3 kHz the beam narrows to +-42 degrees at -6 dB, and at 5 kHz the -6 dB beam is +-24 degrees, with a null at 44 degrees and a side lobe beyond it (peak -17.6 dB, the classic first side lobe of a piston).
sidelobe_dB = max(DdB(3, abs(theta) > deg2rad(theta0_5k)))
sidelobe_dB = -17.5702

Problem 2 - Radiated power of a baffled driver

Given (L_E ignored):
S_D = 500e-4 % cone area, 500 cm^2 [m^2]
S_D = 0.0500
Bl = 10 % force factor [Tm]
Bl = 10
R_E = 5 % coil resistance [ohm]
R_E = 5
M_MS = 0.100 % moving mass incl. air load, 100 g [kg]
M_MS = 0.1000
E_g = 1 % generator voltage amplitude [V]
E_g = 1
Equivalent piston radius:
a = sqrt(S_D/pi) % [m]
a = 0.1262

Problem 2a - Volume velocity above resonance (mass control)

Above f_S the cone is mass controlled: the suspension spring and the damping no longer matter. With L_E ignored, and the back-EMF small compared with E_g in this region (checked below), the coil current is E_g/R_E and Newton gives
For these numbers the constant is exactly 1:
U_const = S_D*Bl*E_g/(M_MS*R_E) % [m^3/s * rad/s], so |U| = 1/omega
U_const = 1
A volume velocity falling as 1/omega is a constant volume acceleration, which is exactly what slide 9 asks for to radiate a constant power from a small source.
Check of the back-EMF assumption. The full mass-controlled current is E_g / (R_E + (Bl)^2/(j omega M_MS)); the motional term is small once omega >> (Bl)^2/(R_E M_MS):
f_emf = Bl^2/(R_E*M_MS)/(2*pi) % [Hz]
f_emf = 31.8310
That is 32 Hz, so the approximation is good from about 100 Hz up (at 100 Hz the motional term is 0.32 R_E, which costs 0.4 dB). The 1/omega law is the textbook "mass-controlled" result and the sheet asks for exactly that.

Problem 2b - Radiated power: exact Re(Z_AR) vs. the network

f = logspace(log10(20), log10(20000), 600);
w = 2*pi*f;
k = w/c;
U = U_const./(1j*w); % from 2a
Exact (analytical) real part for the piston in an infinite baffle:
ReZ_exact = rho*c/(pi*a^2) * (1 - besselj(1, 2*k*a)./(k*a));
Network approximation (Lecture 3, baffled piston): M_A1 in parallel with [R_A2 + (R_A1 parallel C_A1)]:
M_A1 = 8*rho/(3*pi^2*a)
M_A1 = 2.5700
R_A1 = 0.441*rho*c/(pi*a^2)
R_A1 = 3.6409e+03
R_A2 = rho*c/(pi*a^2)
R_A2 = 8.2560e+03
C_A1 = 5.94*a^3/(rho*c^2)
C_A1 = 8.3988e-08
Z_RC = R_A1./(1 + 1j*w*R_A1*C_A1); % R_A1 || C_A1
Z_net = (1j*w*M_A1 .* (R_A2 + Z_RC)) ./ (1j*w*M_A1 + R_A2 + Z_RC);
ReZ_net = real(Z_net);
Power with both:
P_exact = 0.5*ReZ_exact.*abs(U).^2;
P_net = 0.5*ReZ_net.*abs(U).^2;
Low-frequency limit. For ka << 1, 1 - J_1(2ka)/(ka) is about (ka)^2/2, so Re(Z_AR) is about rho omega^2/(2 pi c): twice the free-field monopole of slide 9, because the baffle confines the power to a half-space. With U = 1/omega the omegas cancel:
P_LF = rho/(4*pi*c) % [W], flat
P_LF = 2.7760e-04
P_LF_dB = 10*log10(P_LF/1e-12) % [dB re 1 pW]
P_LF_dB = 84.4341
High-frequency limit. For ka >> 1, Re(Z_AR) tends to rho c/S_D (a plane wave over the cone area) and the power falls as 1/omega^2, i.e. 6 dB/octave. The knee is where the two asymptotes meet:
f_knee = sqrt(2)*c/(2*pi*a) % [Hz]
f_knee = 613.7387
fig2 = figure('Name', 'L11_P2_power');
theme(fig2, 'light');
semilogx(f, 10*log10(P_exact/1e-12), 'LineWidth', 1.6); hold on
semilogx(f, 10*log10(P_net/1e-12), '--', 'LineWidth', 1.6);
yline(P_LF_dB, ':', 'rho/(4 pi c)');
xline(f_knee, ':', sprintf('ka = sqrt 2 (%.0f Hz)', f_knee));
hold off; grid on
xlabel('Frequency [Hz]'); ylabel('P_A [dB re 1 pW]');
legend('exact Re(Z_{AR}) (Bessel)', 'network M_{A1}, R_{A1}, R_{A2}, C_{A1}', 'Location', 'southwest');
title('Problem 2b: radiated power, 1 V, mass-controlled region');
xlim([20 20000]); ylim([P_LF_dB-50 P_LF_dB+5]);
if saveFigs, exportgraphics(fig2, fullfile(imgDir, 'L11_P2_power.png'), 'Resolution', 150); end
How close is the network? Largest dB difference, below and above the knee:
dP = 10*log10(P_net./P_exact);
max_dev_below_knee = max(abs(dP(f < f_knee))) % [dB]
max_dev_below_knee = 0.3564
max_dev_overall = max(abs(dP)) % [dB]
max_dev_overall = 0.6334
The network is a smooth fit: it has the right low- and high-frequency asymptotes and is within a fraction of a dB through the knee, but it cannot reproduce the small ripple of the exact curve above ka = 2 (the J_1(2ka) oscillation). For a loudspeaker model that ripple is irrelevant.

Problem 2c - Efficiency

Electrical input power: in the mass-controlled region the current is E_g/R_E and all input power is dissipated in R_E:
P_E = 0.5*E_g^2/R_E % [W]
P_E = 0.1000
Efficiency, in the flat (low-frequency, mass-controlled) region:
eta0 = P_LF/P_E
eta0 = 0.0028
eta0_formula = rho*Bl^2*S_D^2/(2*pi*c*R_E*M_MS^2)
eta0_formula = 0.0028
eta0_percent = 100*eta0
eta0_percent = 0.2776
About 0.28 %: typical for a direct-radiator woofer (0.1-1 %). The formula is the reference efficiency of Lecture 7. Above the knee the efficiency falls with the power, 6 dB/octave:
eta = P_exact/P_E;
fig3 = figure('Name', 'L11_P2_efficiency');
theme(fig3, 'light');
semilogx(f, 100*eta, 'LineWidth', 1.6); grid on
xlabel('Frequency [Hz]'); ylabel('\eta [%]');
title(sprintf('Problem 2c: efficiency, \\eta_0 = %.3f %%', eta0_percent));
xlim([20 20000]);

Problem 3 - Cabinet diffraction with diffrac.m (slides 29-39)

diffrac(corners, r, angles, source_radius, fs) implements Terai's thin- baffle model of slide 32: the direct sound from the source plus a line of edge sources along the baffle rim, each delayed by its path and with a sign inversion. It returns dB re the free field: an infinite baffle would be +6 dB at all frequencies. (It uses c = 343 m/s internally.)
Hand prediction for the centred circle, on axis. Every edge point is at the same distance, so the whole rim arrives at once and the effect is strongest. The extra path of the diffracted wave is
and because the edge inverts the wave, the diffracted wave adds when Delta = lambda/2 (and 3/2, 5/2 ...) and cancels when Delta = lambda:
R_b = 0.30 % baffle radius [m]
R_b = 0.3000
r_obs = 2 % observation distance [m]
r_obs = 2
Delta = R_b + sqrt(r_obs^2 + R_b^2) - r_obs % [m]
Delta = 0.3224
f_max1 = 343/(2*Delta) % first peak [Hz]
f_max1 = 531.9894
f_min1 = 343/Delta % first dip [Hz]
f_min1 = 1.0640e+03
Below about f_max1/2 the baffle is too small to matter: the response sits near 0 dB (free field, the sound wraps round). Well above, it oscillates around +6 dB (the baffle step).

Problem 3a - Point source in the centre of a 30 cm circular baffle

A circle is a polygon with many corners (the help asks for > 100). source_radius = 1 mm makes it effectively a monopole:
phi = linspace(0, 2*pi, 201)';
circ = [R_b*cos(phi) R_b*sin(phi)];
angles3 = [0 0; 30 0; 60 0]; % [azimuth elevation] in degrees
[t3, h3, f3, H3] = diffrac(circ, r_obs, angles3, 0.001, 44100);
diffrac draws its own figures (edge/source geometry, then impulse and frequency response per angle). The three angles together:
fig4 = figure('Name', 'L11_P3a_circle');
theme(fig4, 'light');
semilogx(f3, H3, 'LineWidth', 1.3); grid on
xline([f_max1 f_min1], ':', {'\Delta = \lambda/2', '\Delta = \lambda'});
xlabel('Frequency [Hz]'); ylabel('dB re free field');
legend('0^\circ (on axis)', '30^\circ', '60^\circ', 'Location', 'northwest');
title('Problem 3a: monopole in the centre of a circular baffle, R = 30 cm, r = 2 m');
xlim([50 20000]); ylim([-10 14]);
if saveFigs, exportgraphics(fig4, fullfile(imgDir, 'L11_P3a_circle.png'), 'Resolution', 150); end
Read off the on-axis peak and dip and compare with the hand prediction:
band = f3 > 200 & f3 < 3000;
fb = f3(band); Hb = H3(band, 1);
[pk, ipk] = max(Hb); f_pk = fb(ipk)
f_pk = 538.3301
pk_dB = pk
pk_dB = 9.9429
[dp, idp] = min(Hb(fb > f_pk)); fbb = fb(fb > f_pk); f_dp = fbb(idp)
f_dp = 1.0767e+03
dp_dB = dp
dp_dB = -1.3019
  • On axis the edge contributions all arrive together, so the ripple is large: a peak of +9.9 dB at Delta = lambda/2 (538 Hz) and a dip to -1.3 dB at Delta = lambda (1.08 kHz), 11 dB below the peak, repeating up the band around the +6 dB baffle step (slide 31).
  • At 30 and 60 degrees the path to each edge point is different, the diffracted arrivals smear out over time, and the ripple shrinks. Off axis is smoother: the symmetric, centred source is the worst case for the on-axis response.

Problem 3b - Source off centre

diffrac always puts the source at (0,0), so moving the source is done by moving the baffle the other way. Shift the circle by 10 cm in x and 5 cm in y:
offset = [0.10 0.05]
offset = 1×2
0.1000 0.0500
[~, ~, fb3, Hoff] = diffrac(circ + offset, r_obs, angles3, 0.001, 44100);
fig5 = figure('Name', 'L11_P3b_offset');
theme(fig5, 'light');
semilogx(f3, H3(:,1), 'LineWidth', 1.3); hold on
semilogx(fb3, Hoff, 'LineWidth', 1.3); hold off; grid on
xlabel('Frequency [Hz]'); ylabel('dB re free field');
legend('centred, 0^\circ', 'offset, 0^\circ', 'offset, 30^\circ', 'offset, 60^\circ', 'Location', 'northwest');
title('Problem 3b: source 11 cm off centre on the same circle');
xlim([50 20000]); ylim([-10 14]);
if saveFigs, exportgraphics(fig5, fullfile(imgDir, 'L11_P3b_offset.png'), 'Resolution', 150); end
The edge distances now range from 19 to 41 cm, so the diffracted wave is spread out in time and the deep on-axis notches are filled in. The step from 0 to +6 dB is still there (the baffle is the same size), but the ripple on top is halved (11.2 -> 5.1 dB, 300 Hz-5 kHz): this is why drivers are placed off centre (slide 40, "asymmetric driver placement").
ripple_centred = max(H3(f3>300 & f3<5000,1)) - min(H3(f3>300 & f3<5000,1)) % [dB]
ripple_centred = 11.2448
ripple_offset = max(Hoff(fb3>300 & fb3<5000,1)) - min(Hoff(fb3>300 & fb3<5000,1)) % [dB]
ripple_offset = 5.1280

Problem 3c - Your own baffle shapes

Two typical cabinet fronts, same source (a 5 cm piston rather than a point, like a real tweeter/midrange), on axis:
  • a 20 x 35 cm rectangle with the driver centred left-right and 7.5 cm above the middle (the typical "two-way" front),
  • the same rectangle with the driver also 3 cm off the left-right centre,
  • the same outline with 5 cm chamfered corners (a cheap way to soften the edges).
W = 0.20; Hh = 0.35; yoff = 0.075; xoff = 0.03;
rect = [ W/2 Hh/2; W/2 -Hh/2; -W/2 -Hh/2; -W/2 Hh/2];
ch = 0.05;
cham = [ W/2 Hh/2-ch; W/2 -Hh/2+ch; W/2-ch -Hh/2; -W/2+ch -Hh/2; ...
-W/2 -Hh/2+ch; -W/2 Hh/2-ch; -W/2+ch Hh/2; W/2-ch Hh/2];
shapes = {rect - [0 yoff], rect - [xoff yoff], cham - [xoff yoff]};
names = {'rectangle, centred in x', 'rectangle, 3 cm off in x', 'chamfered, 3 cm off in x'};
[~, ~, fs3, H_rect] = diffrac(shapes{1}, r_obs, [0 0], 0.025, 44100);
[~, ~, ~, H_off] = diffrac(shapes{2}, r_obs, [0 0], 0.025, 44100);
[~, ~, ~, H_cham] = diffrac(shapes{3}, r_obs, [0 0], 0.025, 44100);
Hs = [H_rect H_off H_cham];
fig6 = figure('Name', 'L11_P3c_shapes');
theme(fig6, 'light');
semilogx(fs3, Hs, 'LineWidth', 1.3); grid on
xlabel('Frequency [Hz]'); ylabel('dB re free field');
legend(names, 'Location', 'northwest');
title('Problem 3c: 20 x 35 cm front, 5 cm piston, on axis, r = 2 m');
xlim([100 20000]); ylim([-10 14]);
if saveFigs, exportgraphics(fig6, fullfile(imgDir, 'L11_P3c_shapes.png'), 'Resolution', 150); end
What to look for: the narrow front puts the baffle step higher (about c/(pi W) to c/(pi H), several hundred Hz) than the 60 cm circle. Moving the driver off the left-right symmetry line makes the two side edges arrive at different times and reduces the ripple. Chamfers barely help in this thin-baffle model, because the edge is still a sharp line of sources; real roundovers work by making the edge gradual over a distance comparable with the wavelength (slide 40), which diffrac cannot represent. Result: ripple 3.4 dB centred, 2.8 dB off centre, 2.8 dB chamfered (500 Hz-8 kHz): the offset helps, the chamfer does not.
mid = fs3>500 & fs3<8000;
ripple_shapes = max(Hs(mid,:)) - min(Hs(mid,:)) % [dB] rect, offset, chamfered
ripple_shapes = 1×3
3.4018 2.8032 2.8399
